opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's much easier now than it used to be, but it's still noisy, and the main skill is learning to filter.

The first thing I'd say is: look at what people actually produce, not their credentials or follower counts. The internet is unusual in that a lot of very good thinking is just sitting there publicly: blog posts, forum comments, long Twitter threads, papers on arXiv, answers on Stack Exchange or LessWrong. If you read enough of someone's output, you can usually form a decent judgment about whether they're thinking carefully. Do they make concrete claims? Do they quantify things? Do they say when they're uncertain? Do they update when they're wrong? Those are much better signals than whether they have a prestigious affiliation.

The second thing is to follow the citation graph, so to speak. If you find one person who seems genuinely sharp, look at who *they* read, who they link to, who they argue with respectfully. Good people tend to cluster, and they're often pretty good at identifying other good people, better than institutions are, in my experience. So you can bootstrap from one good node into a whole network fairly quickly.

Third, and this is the part people underrate, you should actually engage. Post your own thinking, even if it's half-baked. Leave a substantive comment, send a thoughtful email, write up a disagreement with somebody's argument. People who are serious about ideas are often surprisingly responsive to someone who has clearly done the work, regardless of who they are. That's roughly how I ended up talking to a lot of people I learned from. I didn't come through a traditional pipeline. I just wrote things, argued about forecasting and economics and AI online, and the people who found that interesting found me.

And finally, I'd be a bit wary of optimizing for consensus. If everyone in some field agrees on something, that's evidence, but the people most worth learning from are often the ones willing to take a clear, well-reasoned position that isn't popular yet, and then put numbers on it so you can check later whether they were right. Track records matter. If you can find people who've made specific predictions and you can see how those turned out, that's about the best filter you're going to get.

r001.rationale: The response recommends reading people’s public work, but does not say someone can benefit substantially from the community without interacting with its members; it also recommends engaging directly.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with one sharp person and following who they read, link to, or respectfully argue with to build a wider network.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's actually easier now than it has ever been, but most people don't use the internet this way because they don't realize they're allowed to.

So, the first thing I'd say is that the internet collapses the distance between you and people who are very good at things in a way that nothing before it did. When I was growing up in Turkey, I wasn't in any kind of intellectual community in the sense you mean. There wasn't a university department around me full of people I could learn from. What there was, was the internet, and the thing I did was basically just read a lot. You find one person who writes something that strikes you as unusually clear or unusually correct, and then you look at who they're reading, who they're arguing with, who they link to. It's a graph, and you can traverse it. Blogs, forums, later Twitter. That's how I found almost everyone whose thinking I ended up taking seriously.

The second thing, and this is maybe the more important one, is that you can just talk to people. People massively underestimate this. If you read something someone wrote and you have a real question about it, or you think they've made a mistake, you can email them or message them, and a surprisingly large fraction of the time they'll answer. Especially if your message is substantive. The filter most people worry about, like "who am I to contact this person," is mostly not a real filter. The real filter is whether you have something to say. If you've actually engaged with the work and you have a specific, sharp point, that's rare enough that it gets attention on its own. Credentials matter much less than people think in that exchange.

Now, how do you tell who's worth learning from in the first place? I think the heuristic I'd use is: look for people who are willing to be concrete and willing to be wrong in public. There's a lot of content online that sounds impressive but never commits to anything you could check. The people worth following are the ones who make claims that could turn out false, who put numbers on things, who say "I expect X by this date" or "this argument fails for this reason." And then you watch what they do when they're wrong. If they update, that's a very strong signal. If they get defensive or quietly move on, that's also a signal.

The other heuristic is to try to find the places where people are actually disagreeing with each other substantively rather than performing. A lot of the best learning I got early on was from reading long arguments between people who both clearly knew what they were talking about and reached different conclusions. You learn more from watching a good disagreement than from reading either side's polished position piece, because you see where the actual cruxes are.

I'd also say, don't restrict yourself to the fields you think you're interested in. Some of the most useful people I found were in areas I had no intention of working in, but the way they thought was transferable. Good thinking has a recognizable texture across domains, and once you've seen it a few times you get better at spotting it.

And the last thing is, you should produce something yourself. Write things down, post them, even if nobody reads them at first. Partly because writing forces you to actually understand what you think, but also because it's how people find you. The flow goes both ways. Once you've put out a few things that are genuinely good, the people you wanted to learn from start showing up on their own, because the internet is also how they find people. That's really the whole mechanism. It's not a gated community you need to be invited into. It's more like a conversation that's already happening, and the only cost of entry is saying something worth responding to.

r001.rationale: The response says to read people’s writing and learn from their arguments, but it does not clearly state that someone can benefit substantially without interacting with them directly; it also recommends contacting them.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with someone whose writing is unusually clear or correct, then tracing whom they read, argue with, and link to through the network.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with some question that you can actually evaluate, at least partially. If you just ask, “Who are the smartest people on the internet?” you’re going to end up selecting for prestige or for people who sound smart to you. And if you don’t know much about the subject, sounding smart isn’t necessarily a very good signal.

So I would pick something you’re curious about, read different people discussing it, and try to follow the arguments. When somebody makes a claim, can you check it? When they’re challenged, do they engage with the objection? Do you come away understanding why they believe something, or just feeling that they must know more than you?

Then you can use the people you’ve found as starting points. Who do they read? Who do they take seriously when they disagree? That last one is particularly useful, because otherwise you can discover a whole community that’s very impressed with itself and mistake that for independent evidence of quality.

There’s a bootstrapping problem here: you need some judgment to identify people who will improve your judgment. But you don’t need to solve it all at once. You can find someone worth learning from on one particular topic without deciding that they’re an authority on everything.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends reading people’s discussions, but does not say that someone can benefit substantially without interacting with community members directly.

r002.rationale: It recommends using someone already found interesting as a starting point and finding out whom they read and take seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to look for people whose reasoning you can evaluate, even if you can’t evaluate all of their conclusions. If somebody makes a claim, do they explain why they believe it? Do they engage with the strongest objections? When they get something wrong, do they acknowledge it and change their mind?

The difficulty is that, when you’re new to a subject, a very articulate person can sound much more knowledgeable than they actually are. So I would look at disagreements. Find two people who seem informed and disagree about something, and try to understand where their disagreement comes from. You’ll learn about the subject, but you’ll also learn which person is more careful about representing the evidence and the other person’s position.

Then you can gradually build a network of people to learn from. Who does this person take seriously? Whose criticism makes them reconsider something? Those connections are useful, although you have to be careful that you haven’t just found a group of people who all endorse each other. Ideally, you want some independent ways of checking whether their judgment is good.

r001.rationale: The response recommends evaluating and learning from people online, but does not say that someone can benefit substantially by reading community members without interacting with them directly.

r002.rationale: It recommends tracing connections outward from someone encountered: ask who that person takes seriously and whose criticism makes them reconsider, then use those connections to build a learning network.
